name: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 10 (CLN10 / cathepsin D deficiency)

reference.source: Neurogenetics and inherited metabolic disease references
clinicalPearls: CLN10 is caused by deficiency of cathepsin D, a lysosomal aspartyl protease encoded by CTSD, and is the classic cause of congenital NCL, the earliest-onset and most severe form.

The congenital form presents at or before birth with microcephaly, refractory neonatal seizures often reaching status epilepticus, rigidity and respiratory insufficiency, frequently with death in the neonatal period.
It may be heralded antenatally by reduced foetal movements or abnormal foetal imaging.
Milder CTSD variants cause later-onset disease, including late-infantile, juvenile and even adult-onset phenotypes with retinopathy and progressive neurodegeneration.
Unlike most NCLs, which store subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase, CLN10 and CLN1 accumulate storage material rich in sphingolipid activator proteins (saposins).
Electron microscopy shows granular osmiophilic deposits, the same ultrastructure seen in CLN1.
Because it is an enzyme deficiency, CLN10 can be supported biochemically by demonstrating reduced cathepsin D activity, then confirmed by CTSD genetic testing.
Congenital CLN10 brain imaging shows severe atrophy with cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia and a thin cortex.
reference.pathophysiology: CLN10 disease is an autosomal recessive neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis caused by biallelic variants in CTSD on chromosome 11p15, which encodes cathepsin D, an abundant lysosomal aspartyl protease essential for lysosomal protein turnover and neuronal homeostasis. Deficiency of cathepsin D activity impairs degradation of lysosomal substrates, including sphingolipid activator proteins (saposins), so that, unlike most NCLs which store subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase, CLN10 accumulates storage material rich in saposins A and D, seen ultrastructurally as granular osmiophilic deposits identical to those of CLN1. The degree of residual enzyme activity governs the phenotype: complete loss of function produces congenital NCL, the earliest and most severe form with antenatal or neonatal onset, whereas partial activity yields attenuated late-infantile, juvenile or adult-onset disease with retinopathy and progressive neurodegeneration. Widespread neuronal loss with severe brain atrophy underlies the clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: CLN1 (PPT1) NCL, which shares granular osmiophilic deposits and saposin storage
Other causes of congenital microcephaly with neonatal seizures (congenital infection, brain malformation, other metabolic encephalopathies)
CLN2, CLN5, CLN6, CLN7 and CLN8 (for the later-onset CTSD phenotypes)
Early infantile epileptic encephalopathies of other genetic cause
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing (CTSD sequencing, NCL gene panel or exome sequencing)
Cathepsin D enzyme activity assay in fibroblasts or leucocytes
Brain MRI for severe atrophy with cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia in the congenital form
Electron microscopy demonstrating granular osmiophilic deposits
EEG, which may show a burst-suppression pattern with neonatal seizures in the congenital form
Electroretinography and ophthalmology for retinopathy in later-onset forms
Antenatal imaging and foetal assessment where congenital disease is suspected
redFlags: Congenital microcephaly with refractory neonatal seizures and respiratory failure
Reduced foetal movements or antenatal-onset neurological abnormality
Later-onset progressive visual loss with cognitive and motor regression
reference.prognosis: The congenital cathepsin D-deficiency form is frequently lethal in the neonatal period; later-onset CTSD phenotypes progress over months to years with variable survival. No disease-modifying therapy is licensed; care is supportive, including perinatal palliative care in the congenital form.
pitfalls: Missing CLN10 in a neonate labelled as hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy or congenital infection.
Forgetting that CLN10, like CLN1, stores saposins and shows granular osmiophilic deposits rather than the ATP-synthase-subunit-c and curvilinear pattern of most NCLs.
Assuming all NCLs are childhood-onset; CTSD has adult-onset forms.
Overlooking the cathepsin D enzyme assay that can rapidly support the diagnosis.
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists for cathepsin D deficiency, so management is supportive and, in the congenital form, centred on perinatal palliative care

Provide neonatal supportive care in the congenital form, including respiratory support for respiratory insufficiency and control of refractory neonatal seizures and status epilepticus with antiepileptic drugs and benzodiazepines
Control seizures and myoclonus with antiepileptic drugs in later-onset phenotypes
Support nutrition and swallowing with tube or gastrostomy feeding as bulbar function declines
Arrange ophthalmology and low-vision support for the retinopathy of later-onset forms
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic medicine, neurology, rehabilitation and palliative care input

Offer genetic counselling, carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis for this autosomal recessive condition, including antenatal counselling where reduced foetal movements or abnormal foetal imaging are found
